nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Scientific Name:  Lagodon rhomboides

Synonyms: Taken from Darcy (1581):
	 	Sparus rhomboides, Linnaeus, 1766
		Sargus rhomboides, Valenciennes, in Cuvier and Valenciennes, 1830
		Diplodus rhomboides, Jordan and Gilbert, 1882
		Lagodon rhomboidalis, Goode and Bean, 1886
		Salema atkinsoni, Fowler, 1940
		Lagodon mercaroris, Delsman, 1941
Common Name: Pinfish
Other Common Names: Bream (particularly Florida Keys), salt-water bream (South Carolina), Fair-maid (Virginia), Spanish porgy (Bermuda), pin perch, sand perch, piggy-perch (parts of Western Gulf of Mexico), sailor`s choice, butterfish, chopa spina, chopa espina (Cuba), sargo (parts of the Florida Keys), sargo selema (Spanish), sar selema (French), poisson beurre (Cajun) (496 1581).

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:	Chordata
	Class:		Actinopterygii
	Order:		Perciformes
	Family:	Sparidae

Note: Superclass Osteichthyes

nodes.title: Juvenile
nodes.body:
Adult: The pinfish has a compressed, oblong body, with a depth approximately 2 times its SL; elevated back; small, nearly horizontal mouth; maxillary slipping under lachimal for most of its length; eight deeply notched, broad incisors anteriorly on edge of each jaw succeeded by two rows of broad, blunt teeth; broad, moderate pelvic fins inserted posteriorly to base of pectorals; long, pointed pectoral fins anterior to the tips of pelvics and extending past origin of the anal fin; anal fin has three sharp, strong spines, second and third of equal measure, and soft part of fin is similar to the dorsal fin; deeply forked caudal fin has 15 rays (branched); small, firm scales extending posteriorly of the caudal peduncle, forming a scaly sheath on the soft part of anal and dorsal fins;  ten scales between dorsal fin and lateral line; long slender sharp dorsal spines;  long, low, continuous dorsal fin, preceded by an antrorse spine;   origin of dorsal fin anterior to bases of pectorals; and a proportionately greater interorbital distance, shorter head, longer snout, and smaller eye with growth (91 312 363 378 1583 1584 1585; as cited in 1581).

Color of the pinfish is as follows:  olive to dark green on dorsal side, silvery blue underneath; dark spot behind head  (dorsal side); four to six dark stripes on side; several light yellow and blue longitudinal stripes along the side; pale blue or plain dorsal fin, with faint brownish-yellow spots and with brownish-yellow distal parts of the spious portion; pale yellow pectoral and caudal fins, which is sometimes faintly barred; brownish yellow anal fin, translucent on basal half; brownish yellow streaks at the middle of pale pelvic fins; adults more brightly colored than the young, which are missing longitudinal stripes but possess distinct dark crossbars (312 846; as cited in 1581).

Similar Species:  Species associated with the pinfish are the: pigfish, Orthopristis chrysoptera; gulf pipefish, Syngnathus scovelli; dusky pipefish, S. floridae; planehead filefish, Monacanthus fispidus; silver jenny, Eucinostomus gula; and silver perch, Bairdiella chrysoura (91 1759).  E. gula and the pinfish are closely related, share ancestral characteristics, and presumably evolved in similar fashion (1759).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body: Overall:  Pinfish occur in coastal waters from as far north as Massachusetts to Mexico.  Rare north of Maryland, the pinfish is considered one of the most common inshore fishes of the Gulf of Mexico (from the Yucatan Peninsula to southern Florida) and the southern Atlantic (496 1581).

nodes.title: By State
nodes.body:
Within Florida-The pinfish is very abundant throughout Florida waters (496 581 664 835 891 1054).  Hastings (1248) found pinfish to be common around man-made platforms off Panama City, FL.  During a one year sampling period, pinfish represented 61% of all trawlable ichthyofauna in Apalachee Bay, FL (679).  In the nearshore zone of St. Andrew Bay, FL, four species (Lagodon rhomboides, Menidia beryllina, Eucinostomus argenteus, and Leiostomus xanthurus) made up 94.5% of the total catch (1031).  In various collections in Florida, the abundance of pinfish, in relation to other species, ranked number one in Cedar Key, two at Marco Island, three in a coastal marsh in northwest FL, fourth in  St. Andrew Bay, and 5th along the west coast of Everglades National Park (581 1442 1596 1598 1776).  Pinfish are commonly collected in the shallows of McKay Bay, primarily from March through August (853).  Pinfish are also reported as one of the most abundant species found in the Jupiter Inlet area (887), in Florida Bay (702 1373 1431 1435 1442).
	Pinfish are most abundant in areas of dense mixed plant communities containing large amounts of Halodule and Syringodium (851 1243 1431).  Along south Florida`s Gulf coast, almost 50% of the estuarine bottoms are covered by submerged aquatic vegetation, presumably responsible for the high abundance of pinfish in this area (496).

Other Areas: Pinfish are very abundant throughout the northern Gulf of Mexico with areas of concentration being found in Texas and Louisiana, except in the very turbid brackish waters of western Louisiana (327).  In the Phillips Island and Bogue Sound estuary beds near Beaufort, NC, pinfish accounted for 45 and 68% of the production and 26.7 and 62.6% of the respiration, respectively (1632).  Within an artificial reef off Murrells Inlet, SC, the pinfish was one of the most abundant species found in 11 m depth water (1744).
By Stock:  There are no localized stock or subspecies of pinfish (91), considered a morphospecies (1581).  There are no differences in sexual or population karyotypes between northern Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic populations (218).  Caldwell (91) observed that a variation in the number of lateral line scales differed in regions, attributable to environmental factors and not genetics.  Furthermore, no significant differences between shallow and deep water specimens were found (1581).

nodes.title: By Estuary
nodes.body:
Indian River Lagoon:  Gilmore (993) found pinfish ranked third in number and first in percent occurrence in the central part of the Indian River Lagoon.
Tampa Bay:  Pinfish consisted of 13.3% of total catch between Tampa Bay and Dry Tortugas, FL in 9-35 m water depth (1581) (also Sarasota Bay).
Florida Bay:  Pinfish ranked first in spiny-rayed fish abundance in Florida Bay (702).

nodes.title: Spatial Strategy
nodes.body:
Egg:  Eggs are marine and neritic (1544 1581).
Larva:  Larvae are estuarine and marine, having been found 20 km offshore (314 1544).  They are pelagic, moving inshore to metamorphose into juveniles (314 1581).
Juvenile:  Juveniles are riverine, estuarine, and marine (1037 1544).  During the winter, juveniles occupy the shallower water of estuaries (91).  Juveniles 1216 mm TL were found in schools of similar size Atlantic croakers (Micropogonias undulatus) and spot (Leiostomus xanthurus) in deeper channels and estuaries near Beaufort, NC (314).  As juveniles increase in size, they are found in a wide variety of habitats:  inshore and offshore; eelgrass flats; turtlegrass flats; around piers, jetties, and pilings; canals; river mouths; intertidal pools; saltmarshes (91 157 314 581 679 680 789 1096 1248 1586 1587 1588 1590 1591 1592 1593 1596).
Young-of-Year:  At the end of their first summer, young-of-the-year pinfish move offshore to deeper water (1029 1596).
Adult:  Adults are found in a variety of habitats, with a preference for protected waters (1581).  Pinfish are found inshore: over vegetated flats and rocky substrates; around pilings, wharves, and jetties; in salt marshes, canals, ponds, and creeks; along beaches and mangrove shores; channels and passes for larger individuals; and sometimes over sandy bottoms (91 94 157 294 378 581 664 684 694 789 1167 1248 1286 1461 1597 1598 1599 1600 1601).  They have been collected in Florida Bay in both seagrass beds and among mangrove prop roots, but much more abundant in the seagrass areas (724).  Pinfish may rely on salt marshes for protective cover and not for food resources (1762).  Pinfish are abundant in areas with Halodule, Syringodium, and/or Thalassia (1431 1448).

Pinfish are marine to riverine (835), preferring protected waters and depth of 30-50 m in the Gulf (115 223 363), but also described as preferring shallow, vegetated areas (273 516 581 583 694 1431).  Pinfish have been collected in waters as deep as 92 m (553).  During the winter and cooler months, pinfish are found offshore in open-shelf, coastal, and live-bottom areas (223 883 1602 1603).  Greatest abundances of pinfish are found between 55-92 m off Mississippi (223) and <36 m between Tampa Bay and the Dry Tortugas, FL (1604).  In the north western Gulf of Mexico in the winter, pinfish are common over brown shrimp grounds, as deep as 73 m, but not white shrimp grounds (113 303 1581).

Pinfish have adapted to the estuarine habitat by regulating their metabolic expenditure, moving from the seagrass beds to deeper water as unfavorable conditions occur (1607).  Cooler water temperature and darkness have a large effect on pinfish standing crop within a seagrass bed (1607).  A correlation exists between seagrass (Zostera) biomass, fish biomass, and temperature, as fish biomass was highest at maximum temperature and grass biomass (1607).

Larvae begin to move into estuaries from the marine environment when they are 11 mm TL (363).  Hoese (322) reported larvae from December through March at Port Aransas, but did not collect them within the bay.  Late postlarvae and early juveniles appear in Tampa Bay from about December through February (664 1019 1341 1391).

Juveniles migrate to the estuaries during spring and summer.  Juveniles rarely leave the protected areas of vegetated flats except at night when they move into nearby sand flats (678).  When water temperatures exceed 32C in the flats, pinfish move to the cooler, deeper waters of channels (91).  Juveniles and adults migrate out of the estuaries in the fall to their spawning grounds in the mostly deeper Gulf waters (255 553).  Gunter (255) reported that some juveniles remain inshore and Perry (553) found a stable adult population remaining offshore in deep Gulf waters (40-50 fathoms).

Adults tend to congregate in areas rich in food sources, as a positive correlation has been found between abundance and macrophyte biomass (273 1593).  In Buttonwood Canal, FL, pinfish abundance was associated best with season (temperature), as movement to deeper waters offshore, or into channels and basins, occurs during the coldest part of the year to avoid cold temperatures (94 255 294 524 603 702 1029 1032 1286 1581 1587 1591 1592 1595).  Also, pinfish move to deeper waters during the summer to avoid high temperatures (94 1607).  As pinfish get larger, they move to deeper water and sometimes stay there (294).  The differences and changes in depth distribution and size may be due to prey-size selection or the inability of larger pinfish to handle metabolic extremes of shallow water (94).

Pinfish show daily movement as well.  With varying temperatures, daily and seasonal movements may be a result of large fish being unable to handle extra metabolic demands to deal with stress (1607).  Daily migration to deeper water is due more to oxygen than temperature (1611).  During the summer, as a consequence of higher temperatures, hypoxic conditions occur with greater frequency which causes the pinfish to migrate to deeper, cooler water (1611).  The need for oxygen increases with size and the spatial strategy of the pinfish is in large part defined by oxygen availability (1611).

Mobility/Migration (by life stage):
Egg:  Eggs that are fertile are semi-buoyant (1544).  Eggs are presumably planktonic and offshore (614).
Larva:  Larvae are marine to estuarine (1544).  Larvae move into estuarine seagrass beds in North Carolina during January and February (1607).   Larval pinfish move from offshore waters to inshore estuaries and coastal canals during the winter (1167).  Thayer et al (1634) observed larval pinfish began to enter the Newport River Estuary, NC during November
Young-of-Year:  No information available.
Juvenile:  Juveniles are estuarine to riverine (1544).  During the spring and early summer, juvenile pinfish reach a maximum in estuarine seagrass beds in North Carolina, resulting from aging larvae that remained from the winter or a migration to the beds from unvegetated surrounding areas (1607).
During winter, subadult and adult pinfish move offshore, though some remain near shore year-round (314 480 664 694).  Reduced numbers collected in the fall and winter months in Tampa Bay and the Ten Thousand Islands area confirm this migratory pattern (853 1054).  It is unclear if this movement is a result of spawning cues, temperature, or a combination of the two (1581).  These nearshore populations are much smaller in size than summer populations (255 581 1286 1588 1591 1592 1595).

Adult:  Adults are marine to riverine (1544).  They are essentially non-schooling although the forming of compact aggregations has been reported (386).  A correlation exists between seagrass (Zostera) biomass, fish biomass, and temperature, as fish biomass was highest at maximum temperature and grass biomass (1607).

The adults exhibit diurnal activity patterns on the mudbanks of Florida Bay, with activity centered around high tides (852 1432).  Ryan (1449) concluded that the species was diurnally active in Apalachee Bay, Pristas and Trent (1450) had higher catch rates at night in St. Andrews Bay, but Low (1179) caught them throughout the day in Biscayne Bay.

nodes.title: Symbiotic
nodes.body: Schooling: Schooling behavior is observed during feeding, the spawning/winter movement migration, and in young while moving inshore (1581).  In calm waters, young pinfish have been seen schooling with other species, juvenile spot, Leiostomus xanthurus, and Atlantic croaker, Micropogonias undulatus (314).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Substrate:  Adults are found in open waters, vegetated areas, and deeper channels (91 363 516 581 1373).  The preferred substrate of the pinfish is vegetated (581).  Along south Florida`s Gulf coast, almost 50% of the estuarine bottoms are covered by submerged aquatic vegetation, presumably responsible for the high abundance of pinfish in this area (496).  Pinfish also occur over coral, mud, rock, sand, and mixtures of these, but their preference is over vegetated substrates (91 1581).  An absence of a vegetated bottom will lead the pinfish to live around jetties, pilings, rocks, docks, breakwaters, and mangrove roots (91).  Motta et al. (1759) observed the pinfish to forage over sandy substrates and within seagrass beds.

Submerged Vegetation (by life stage):
Vegetation, rather than salinity, is thought to have a greater affect on the distribution of pinfish (561 760).  The most important environmental characteristic influencing distribution is vegetation (91 378), based on feeding (1581).  A correlation exists between seagrass (Zostera) biomass, fish biomass, and temperature, as fish biomass was highest at maximum temperature and grass biomass (1607).

Depth Distribution (by life stage):
Water depth over seagrass beds has little to no effect on the population of pinfish (1607).  However, greatest abundances of pinfish are found between 55-92 m off Mississippi (223) and <36 m between Tampa Bay and the Dry Tortugas, FL (1604).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Egg:  Pinfish eggs are spawned offshore in marine environments.  No preferred temperature is given for pinfish eggs in the literature, since they range from Mexico to Massachusetts.
Larva:  Larvae have been collected in a variety of temperatures in equally various habitats, ranging from offshore to estuarine.  Again, no specific temperature range is stated in the literature for pinfish larvae.
Young-of-Year:  No information available.
Juvenile:  Juveniles are more susceptible to thermal shock if salinity changes with temperature, demonstrating a combination temperature-salinity effect (496).  Again, due to the varied estuarine habitat the juvenile pinfish occupies, no optimal temperature range was found in the literature for this life stage.
Adult:  Pinfish are able to withstand a wide range of temperature (1581).  Pinfish are able to handle lower temperatures than most other species in the same area (314 836 1036).  One study found that pinfish cannot survive below 3.4 C (1757) while another suggests that 6 C is the lower limit (1754).  A low lethal temperature range of 6 - 8 C is also suggested (93).  Pinfish have been killed by low temperatures due to freezes in Texas (253), North Carolina (496), and both coasts of Florida (236 836 1023 1068).

An upper lethal temperature range for pinfish is 31-36.9 C.  Temperatures >35 C are actively avoided (91 93 223 225 1581) and feeding stops at temperatures above 36 C (1754).  Florida records include: 18.9-36.9 C at Cedar Key (91), 10.0-32.5 C in Tampa Bay (664),16.0-30.0 C  in Everglades National Park (702 1373), 19.9-37.9 C  at Matecumbe Key (800), and 18.0-34.0 C  near Jupiter inlet (887).

Water temperature has been suggested as a major factor in the control of emigration to offshore spawning sites.  Emigration may be a function of the constancy of temperature offshore, rather than the degree itself (91).

Increased water temperatures increase the amount of erythrocytes and hemoglobin of pinfish (93 343 561). Extremely high and low temperatures cause pinfish to leave shallow areas for nearby deeper waters, even on a daily bases (94).  Temperature, rather than salinity, was found to effect feeding rates in pinfish (1629).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Egg:  The literature does not specify a particular salinity range for pinfish eggs.  Since they spawn offshore, salinities typical of the marine environment, approximately 35 ppt, would be a safe assumption.
Larva:  Collection of larvae in the eastern Gulf of Mexico occurred in salinities between 33-36 ppt (1581).
Young-of-Year:  No information available.
Juvenile:  Gunter (255) found no correlation between fish size and salinity though juveniles are found to occur in lower salinities than adults (789).  Heavy rains, reducing salinity, decreases the abundance of juvenile pinfish in shallow seagrass beds and estuaries (95 789).  Juveniles are more susceptible to thermal shock if salinity changes with temperature, demonstrating a combination temperature-salinity effect (496).
Adult:  Pinfish are found in salinities ranging from 0-75 ppt (294).  Pinfish abundance has been found to be positively correlated with salinity (684 685).  However, vegetation and temperature, rather than salinity, is thought to have a greater affect on the distribution of pinfish (561 760 1581).  Pinfish abundance decreased after heavy rains as salinity dropped 4 ppt on shallow flats along the Texas coast (94).  Colby et al. (1054) found pinfish more abundant at higher salinities.

Pinfish have been collected in Florida at the following salinities:  0.1-37.2 ppt at Cedar Key (91 378), 3.7-35.1 ppt in Tampa Bay (664), 0.1-43.8 ppt in Caloosahatchee River (265), 34.5-37.9 ppt at Matecumbe Key (800), 8.0-43.8 ppt in Everglades  National Park (702 1373),  near freshwater inflows in Apalachee Bay, FL (1594), and 4.5-38.8 ppt near Jupiter Inlet (887).

Elsewhere, highest abundances of pinfish occurred:  5-10 ppt at Bayport, FL (378); above 18 ppt at Horn Island, MS (224); between 23-38 ppt at deeper stations off Mississippi (55-92 m) (223).

If enough calcium is present, pinfish are able to withstand freshwater habitats, as they are capable of extracting sodium in low sodium environments (1622).  The process of sodium extraction relies on chloride-secreting cells, important in electrolyte regulation and allowing the pinfish to tolerate a wide range of salinities (1623).

The salinity effects sustained swimming velocities in pinfish (1786).  At 20 ppt, the highest sustained swimming velocity was observed (1786).  Beyond this concentration, Kloth and Wohlschlag (1786) noticed decreased swimming velocity with increased salinity.

Dissolved Oxygen:  Pinfish oxygen-carrying capacity is related to environmental conditions, increasing with lower dissolved oxygen, higher salinities, and increased activity (93).  Adams (1632) found that at least 90% of the variation in DO consumption may be attributed to temperature and weight.  The lethal DO level is about 1.1 mg/l (94) and a critical oxygen-tension level of 24 mm Hg have been suggested for pinfish (1611).

When compared to permanent salt-marsh species (cyprinodontid and poeciliid fishes) pinfish oxygen consumption per unit body weight was found to be higher (1611).  This high need for oxygen may explain why pinfish avoid shallow hypoxic waters (1611).    Conversely, pinfish are able to detect, then move away from, supersaturated waters as well (1612).

Oxygen consumption decreases with decreasing fish weight, activity, and temperature (1581), of which fish weight is the more important factor (1632; as cited in 1581).  Seasonal changes in DO consumption are primarily resulting from water temperature changes (93).  Juveniles, rather than adults, are responsible for more community production and respiration, especially during the summer, due to their high biomass (1607).

Pinfish show an increase in hemoglobin concentration and red blood cell counts, and a decrease in hematocrit and mean erythrocyte volume, at high temperatures (95).  Under experimental conditions, blood concentration increases when acclimated to high salinity, low oxygen, and exercise (95).  Changes in blood oxygen capacity are important to seasonal alteration of oxygen transport, but more important to respiratory demand (95).

Turbidity:  In Louisiana, pinfish avoided highly turbid waters (327).  Turbidity, in conjunction with lower salinity, may be responsible for the pinfish movements away from water influenced by heavy rain and a subsequent decrease in salinity (94 789).  Ingle (1613), however, finds that turbidity does not greatly affect pinfish, as they were found around an active dredge.

nodes.title: Floating Habitat
nodes.body:
pH:  No information available.

Light/Photoperiod:  Light conditions, influenced by the time of day and turbidity, were responsible for the diel distribution observed in pinfish in one study (1612, as cited in 496).  70% of the pinfish catch in the study by Thayer et al. (1781, as cited in 496) were landed at night.  Juvenile pinfish feed more commonly during the midday hours (380).  Pinfish react to visual stimuli more so than auditory (1782, as cited in 496).

nodes.title: Ammonia
nodes.body: Currents/Tides:  Pinfish react quickly to pressure changes, however small, and are well adapt in reacting to tidal changes to maintain buoyancy (496).

nodes.title: Trophic Mode
nodes.body:
Eating:  Pinfish consume a wide range of prey throughout the course of their lives, but may be selective feeders in particular areas during certain life stages (1581).  Pinfish have shown to be planktivorous, omnivorous, strictly carnivorous, and strictly herbivorous across different developmental stages, times, and places, but as a species, they are considered omnivorous (679 1581).  Changes in food habits are a result of changing mouth morphology and detention and the relative abundances of food organisms and macrophyte standing crops (1591).

Larva:  Larvae are visual planktivores and feed more actively in areas of mild to no current (380 1624 1625).  Feeding occurs primarily during the day with peak gut content around noon (380 1624 1625).  Kjelson et al. (1624) found larval (18 mm TL) gut capacity to be approximately thirty-seven 650 sm copepods (1624).  Larval pinfish have a significant effect in reducing zooplankton masses and in turn, it is zooplankton abundances that control the survival success of the pinfish during the larval/juvenile transition (1634).

Juvenile:  Juveniles are planktivores, moving to algae and benthic organisms as they get older (697 1167 1626).  The pinfish is an obligate carnivore until the length of 35 mm SL (679).  The shift in diet as pinfish grow may be the result of changing plant abundance and/or protection of prey by vegetation (679).  Juveniles feed diurnally, commonly around seagrass blades (678 1625 1595 1096).

Juveniles <39 mm SL capture prey mainly by suction or ram-feeding (striking with snout and stunning) while >40 mm SL individuals are more apt in capturing prey by biting (1761).  Increases in mouth size and changes in detention influences prey size selectivity and ultimately estuarine trophic relationship (1761).

Adult:  Adults are considered generalists, feeding on vegetated substrates and scraping epifaunal invertebrates from hard substrates (163 679 1248 1627 1628).  Increased algal consumption in larger size classes shows an ontogenetic shift related to seasonal increases in algal abundance (1167).  Teeth are short and blunt and perfect for grazing (91).  Adult pinfish, grazing on seagrass, occasionally turn laterally to feed (1595).  Stanford (1628) observed pinfish turning to an angle of 25 degrees from the horizontal when feeding.

Peak feeding occurs during the summer to early fall, sort of a preparation for spawning and overwintering as a drop in feeding activity is observed during this period (273).  Pinfish are diurnal species, with increased activity at dawn and dusk (852).  In Florida Bay, the pinfish has been observed to center their activity on the banks around high tide, predominantly on the second rise and first fall stages (852).

The habitat characteristics and predator/prey relationships are determining factors in feeding behavior (680 1750). Prey selection depends on density of prey, species of prey, density of seagrass blades, species of seagrass blades, size of prey, accessibility of prey, and the life stage and size of pinfish (680 1587 1591 1592).  Main (1740) found that natural prey selection is dependent upon prey accessibility, while predator preference was determined a nonfactor in feeding.  Prey visibility, due to size and mobility, is the primary determinant in feeding (1740).  Live prey has been found to attract pinfish more frequently than dead organisms (1741).

Food is found visually and through chemoreception (1595 1628 1735 1741).  Bryan et al. (1735) performed an experiment showing that body wall extracts from various species of echinoderms embedded in alginate pellets caused a significant feeding deterrence in pinfish (1735). A combination of amino acids in shrimp extract were found to be responsible for illiciting feeding behavior in pinfish (1751).  A mixture that contained aspartic acid, glycine, glutamine, isoleucine, phenylalanine, and betaine was concluded as responsible for feeding response of pinfish, with betaine accounting for 20-25% of activity response (1751).  Carr et al. (1753) found that extracts from organisms produced feeding activity in pinfish as well.  The most activity was caused by (in descending order) pink shrimp, blue crab, mullet, oyster, whelk, clam, and sea urchin (1753).  Lindquist and Hay (1749) found that pinfish can learn avoidance behavior from chemoreception by introducing them to a distasteful invertebrate not associated with them in the wild.

Food Items (by life stage):
Larva:  Larvae <20 mm SL consume copepods and ichthyoplankton, with prey size increasing as larvae grow (98 380 679 1595 1620 1624 1625 1626).  Of the larvae sampled in the Newport River Estuary, NC, 76 - 99% of total gut contents in the stomachs of larval pinfish were copepods from four taxa; Centopages, Temora, Acartia, and Harpacticoida (1624).  Kjelson et al (1624) found that a pinfish 18 mm in length had a gut capacity of 37 copepods.  A transition from copepods to oligochaetes, polychaetes, and amphipods was observed in larvae 16 - 20 mm SL (1167).  Larvae found in channels contained less copepods than those found nearshore (380 1624 1625).  Adams (1620) observed that pinfish over 35 mm in length tend to shift their diet from copepods to detritus. The daily ration estimate as a percentage of wet body weight of the larvae from the Newport River Estuary was 4.9% (1624), while postlarval estimate was 9% (380).  Food evacuation rates vary with amount of food in the gut (1634).  As the pinfish grows in size, the size of their prey increases as well (380).

Young-of-Year:  No information available.

Juvenile:  Young juveniles feed primarily on harpacticoid copepods, shrimp postlarvae, amphipods, invertebrate eggs, mysids, polychaetes, oligochaetes, and detritus (98 581 680 697 1167 1587 1620 1626).  Older and larger juveniles are considered omnivorous, with increasing importance of plant matter and benthic organisms as the pinfish grows (680 1167 1581 1626).

Luczkovich and Stellwag (1764) found a 10-fold increase in plant material in the intestinal tract of juveniles >40 mm SL, in comparison to individuals <40 mm SL.  Adams (1620) found that once pinfish reach 70 mm, polychaetes and plant material become increasingly more important in their omnivorous diet.  18% of the diet of juvenile pinfish in shallow water estuaries near Beaufort, NC was undigested eelgrass, eelgrass seeds (minimal abundance), and filamentous algae (1620).

Adult:   Adults are reported to be omnivorous, with plant material as a large component of the diet (679 834).  Prey is a function of number and weight (1785).  On the whole, the diet of an adult pinfish is one-half plant material and one-half animal (1785).  The percentage of this diet shifts from an animal dominated diet in the spring to a plant material dominated diet in the late spring/early summer (1785).  Importance of plant material increases as 23% of the diet of adult pinfish in shallow water estuaries near Beaufort, NC was undigested eelgrass, eelgrass seeds, and filamentous algae (1620).  Weinstien et al. (720) observed that 30-40% of the gut contents of adult pinfish to be plant matter.

The shift to herbivory in adults may not be one of choice (1785).  The shift to an omnivorous (more herbivorous) diet is due to low densities of preferred animal prey (1785).  Intestinal tract of herbivorous fish are long, to aid in the slow digestive process of plant material, while carnivorous fish tracts are comparatively short (1785).  The pinfish has a V-shaped stomach and a short intestine, consistent with those found in carnivorous fish (1785).  Little to no evidence of cellulose activity was found in pinfish (760, as cited in 1785).  Furthermore, the feeding behavior is very voracious and does not resemble the slow-moving, more docile behavior exhibited by truly herbivorous fish (1785).

The nutritional role of plant material in the diet of pinfish is largely unknown (1783).  Pinfish have low gastric pH, insufficient to lyse plant cell walls (1783).  There is no difference in growth when comparing individuals with a carnivorous and omnivorous diet (1783).  Consumption of plant material is thought to compensate for low available higher energy food items, maintaining high protein comsumption and growth rates (1783).  Furthermore, the energy saved by not locating and capturing faunal prey may influence the importance of omnivory (1783).

Faunal prey consists of mollusks, shrimps, crabs, copepods, mysids, fish, fish eggs, fish embryos, ctenophores, barnacles, isopods, amphipods, and decapods (98 163 312 678 834 1248 1589 1626 1760 1773), but specific dietary preferences are influenced by food availability and habitat (679).  Main (1774) has reported that the caridean shrimp, Tozeuma carolinense, is underrepresented in the diet of the pinfish.  Evacuation of food is a function of temperature and content (1754).

Amphipods as prey for pinfish in laboratory experiments were more susceptible to predation when on branched seaweeds than on seaweeds with a sheetlike morphology (1755).  Pinfish predation on amphipods is higher during the summer, especially when associated with the seaweed Hypnea, a prefer species for the omnivorous pinfish (1755).  Some invertebrates, included in the diet of the pinfish, may reduce their risk of predation by seeking refuge in a seaweed species unpalatable to pinfish (1755 1766).	Shallow seagrass beds exposed to direct sunlight can result in greater susceptibility to predation by pinfish (1769).  Pinfish, and other herbivores, ate more algae that had been emerged for a period of time (1784).  The emergence caused the algae to produce less amino acid concentrations (1784), known to be responsible for chemical defense.  Cronin and Hay (1769) found that surface levels of UV radiation causes a decrease in chemical defenses by seaweeds.

nodes.title: Repro Mode
nodes.body:
Domain:  Spawning usually occurs offshore, differing geographically, from the late fall to early spring (1581).  Water depth is more important to distance offshore regarding spawning areas, and this will vary with geography (91).

Fertilization:  Pinfish are dioecious with external fertilization, with eggs and sperm released simultaneously (1581).

Spawning Strategy:  Spawning occurs offshore and the young move to inshore estuaries as late larvae or juveniles (1581 1747).  Spawning is probably more related to water depth and temperature than distance offshore (363 496). Most studies in the northern Gulf have indicated that spawning takes place in the fall and winter (82 91 116 255 363 380 581 614).

Life stages are correlated with abundance of prey, seasonal patterns of productivity, and macrophyte species (1591).  For example, larvae appeared in Apalachee Bay, FL during the middle of winter as calanoid copepods were at peak abundance and juveniles were found in seagrass beds during peaks in amphipods and harpacticoid copepods abundances (679).

Reproductive Periodicity:  In North Carolina, the pinfish is suspected to have a spawning period of approximately 5 months (314).  Generally, spawning occurs between October and March (1765).

Parental Care:  Not applicable.

Seasonal Energetics:  Temperature is related to the pinfish immunity system (1605 1606 1608).  Pinfish regulate their metabolism by moving to cooler water during warm, summer months (1607).  The caloric content of pinfish increases with age and varies seasonally (1607 1620 1621).  Carbon and lipid content is greater for adults, as they produce high lipid concentrations in the fall before spawning (1621).

Differences in the weight-specific caloric content are a result of changes in feeding habits and developmental stages (1607 1620).  High caloric contents of adult pinfish in the fall probably reveal a storage of lipids preceding the winter, with possible food shortages (1756; as cited in 1607).

The reproductive process (late August through December) is associated with anabolic and catabolic changes, as serum chemistry parameters increase (1763).
Maturation:  Sparids are predominantly hermaphrodites, yet pinfish are gonochoristic, becoming sexually mature between 80-100 mm TL (273 363 1581 1765). Florida`s Fisheries Independent Monitoring Program (1580) classifies the pinfish as becoming an adult (when over 50% of the size class are sexually mature) at 100 mm TL.  Caldwell (91) stated that only Age II plus individuals were sexually mature, while Hansen (273) suggests that some young-of-the-year individuals are considered sexually mature.  Caldwell (91) reported that pinfish mature during their 2nd year and noted that his smallest mature female was 128mm, but others found that pinfish become sexually mature at sizes ranging from 80-100 mm TL (273 363).  Maturation size is reached during the spawning migration or at the offshore spawning grounds (273).

Fecundity:    Eight pinfish, ranging from 111-152 mm SL, spawned an estimated 7,700 to 39,200 (averaging 21,600) eggs (273).  A 157 mm TL female from Florida collected in November contained an estimated 90,000 eggs (91).

Development (by life stage):
Development is dependent upon temperature, decreasing at lower water temperatures (1581).  Development and growth slow to a halt in the winter, during the coldest part of the year (91 314).  In Texas, the period of maximum growth corresponded, and is correlated, to the period of maximum plant growth (93).

Egg:  At 18C, laboratory reared pinfish eggs reached the blastula stage in approximately 3 h; expanding blastulae were visible within 6 h; late gastrula stage and embryonic axis were evident in 16 h; optic lenses and cups were noticed at 23 h; heartbeat and body movement at 27 h; most hatching occurred in 48 h; emerging larvae measured 2.3 mm TL (363 627 1610).

Larva:  Schimmel (627) observed that pinfish, at 18 C, emerged 48 h after fertilization at a length of 2.3 mm TL.  144 h after fertilization, eye pigmentation appeared (627).  Yolk sac was fifty percent absorbed 15 h after emergence (1610), and completely absorbed when the larvae reached 2.7 mm TL, 96 h after emergence (627).  Total length 96 h after emergence was 2.7 mm TL while at 120 h, TL was 2.5 mm (627).  Malnutrition and infection were suspected to cause the decrease in length and death of larvae after 96 h post-emergence in this particular experiment (627).

Development of the fin rays begins around 4.3 mm SL and is complete by 12.7 mm SL (1775).  The end of the larval stage is reached at 13.9 mm SL, where pigmentation resembles the adult and fin ray development is complete (1775).

Young-of-Year:  Two size classes of pinfish occur.  Caldwell (91) found small Age I pinfish to reach 65-70 mm SL and larger ones to reach 100-110 mm SL by their first year.  Kilby (1167) found in Cedar Key, FL that small pinfish reach 45-80 mm SL and larger ones to reach 100+ mm SL.  After the first year, growth slows to a mean increase of approximately 50 mm SL during the second year and 45 mm SL during the third (91).  Hansen (273, as cited in 1581) describes average daily growth rates on a seasonal basis:

Various weights have been calculated for young-of-the-year pinfish:  4.3 g (581) and 11.0 g (91) in Cedar Key, FL; 7.8 g (93) in Redfish Bay; and 22.3 g (294) in Laguna Madre, TX.

Juvenile:  In Florida, pinfish greater than 10 mm SL and less than 100 mm SL are considered juveniles (1580).  Development varies geographically, depending mainly on temperature.

Adult:  After the first year, growth slows to a mean increase of approximately 50 mm SL during the second year and 45 mm SL during the third (91).  Sexually mature adults have paired gonads that lie dorsal to the intestine (91).  When mature, the testies are pink/flesh colored or white and are slightly distended and the ovaries are yellow with visible opaque eggs (273).

nodes.body:
Egg:  The diameter of pinfish eggs range from 0.90-0.93 mm (627) and 0.99-1.05 mm (363).

Young-of-Year:  No information available.
Juvenile:  Juveniles range in length from 10-100 mm SL (1580).

nodes.title: Aging Structures/Methods
nodes.body: Growth Equations:  Pinfish show averaged growth increments of 80 mm SL through the first year, 50 mm SL through the second, and 45 mm SL through the third (91).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  The pinfish is not considered to be commercially important, but is a common by-catch species of commercial trawlers and is often marketed as a panfish (1581).  There is no direct fishery for the pinfish.  The pinfish is included in the “unclassified” or “industrial fish” categories in commercial catch statistics (1581).  It has potential value as a bait fish, being preyed upon by many commercial and sport fishes, use in pet foods, and use for fish meal (91 1581).  Fillet quality is good, but is usually too small, leaving it as a source for fish meal (1581).  Pinfish are known to produce a high grade oil, as well (314; as stated in 1581).

When sought commercially, catch of pinfish is done so by traps, tramel nets, trawls, gill nets, hook and line, and beach seines (91 1597).  Primary commercial use is for bait (91).  The pinfish is sold as bait for red drum, Sciaenops ocellata, spotted sea trout, Cynoscion nebulosus, tarpon, Megalops atlanticus, snook, Centropomus undecimalis, and various groupers (91 1248; as cited in 1581).

Recreational:  Pinfish are known as a notorious bait stealer frequently caught while fishing for other species (1581).  They are often fished for by children (1544).  Fishery information for the Gulf of Mexico showed a total catch of 10,011,000 pinfish in 1988 (513).

Ecological Role:  The pinfish is an estuarine dependent species.  Pinfish are important predators, prey for larger commercial and recreational species, and contributors to community production, respiration, and consumption (1581).  It is often so abundant and predaceous that it is believed to alter the composition of estuarine epifaunal communities, as seagrass densities are correlated with pinfish abundance (524 127 679 680 993 1581).  Due to its abundance, the pinfish is mentioned and often used in environmental experiments, estuarine ecological studies, and faunal surveys (1581).

In the Bogue Sound bed in North Carolina, the pinfish was responsible for 64% of the total energy consumed by the fish community, 63% of the metabolism, and 68% of the production (1632).

Since the pinfish is omnivorous, changing diets in response to seasonal patterns of prey productivity, the traditional trophic level concept is not applicable (679).  The dominant, most general food web identified for an estuarine ecosystem is turtle grass, grass shrimp (Palaemonetes vulgaris), and pinfish (1745).  Pinfish are a part of a continually changing estuarine food web that have rendered certain models of energetic pathways and predator-prey relationships inoperable (679).

Species Stress:  Saddleback in pinfish might be an indication of low environmental quality in an estuary (1758).
Status:  No information available.
Stock Status:  No information available.

nodes.title: STOCK ENHANCEMENT
nodes.body:
Induced Breeding:  Hormone injection to induce the ova to mature has been performed on pinfish, with a highly variable response (627 1610).  Cardeilhac (1610) has had artificially fertilized pinfish eggs stripped from females.

Rearing:  Pinfish, caught in low salinity waters, are not well adjusted to rearing in similar conditions (1771).

Feeding:  Chamberlain and Strawn (1736) found that winter growth rates of caged pinfish can increase, without feeding, if cages are strategically placed and managed in power plant effluent.

Stocking:  No information available

Disease Control:  No information available

nodes.title: Stock Assessments
nodes.body:
Assessment Name (one or more): No stock assessments have been done on pinfish.
Total Mortality:  No information available.

Natural Mortality:  No information available.

Fishing Mortality:  Pinfish suffer by-catch stress from traps set for blue crabs (1767).  Once the trap is retrieved, the pinfish carcass is not in good shape as abrasions are common from the cage and captured blue crabs consume them (1767).  Pinfish are caught for bait and are often fished for by young anglers (496 1544).  Pinfish are considered good food fish, but are not generally marketed as such, due to their small size (496).

Abundance by Year:  Pinfish abundance is determined by salinity, season (temperature), substrate, vegetation, turbidity, and life stage (1581).  The overriding importance of one or a few factors over the others is uncertain, but typically vegetation and temperature are most commonly thought as determining factors for abundance (1581).

Pinfish are more abundant inshore during the spring and summer months (91).  Sutherland (807) found that in Florida, catch frequencies were highest from April through November, with a peak in the fall, during the month of October.  McGovern and Wenner (1747), however, observed the greatest amount of pinfish caught at creek stations in South Carolina marshes was during the winter when transient species (pinfish considered one) were dominant.

Abundance by Month:  Peak inshore abundance occurs in the late summer and early fall for adults, late spring and early summer for juveniles, and winter to spring for larvae (1607 1631 1634).

Population Abundance:  Peak inshore abundance occurs in the late summer and early fall for adults, late spring and early summer for juveniles, and winter to spring for larvae (1607 1631 1634).  In North Carolina, pinfish numbers are greatest in April while greatest biomass is seen in September (1772).  Along south Florida`s Gulf coast, almost 50% of the estuarine bottoms are covered by submerged aquatic vegetation, presumably responsible for the high abundance of pinfish in this area (496).  Near Beaufort, NC, pinfish numbers were found to be greatest in April, while biomass was greatest in September (1772).  In the Phillips Island and Bogue Sound beds in North Carolina, juvenile pinfish accounted for 57 and 82% of total pinfish production, respectively (1632).  Decrease in density results from excess emigration over immigration and mortality of the resident estuarine population (1607).

Management Regulations:  Currently, there are no management regulations concerning pinfish.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Competition:  Specific competition between pinfish and other species is not proven.  Similar feeding habits have been observed between pinfish and spottail pinfish, Diplodus holbrooki, but direct competition for food does not occur due to differences in morphology (1595).  Even species occupying the same habitat, little dietary overlap is seen between the pinfish and the hardhead catfish, Arius felis, and the gulf pipefish, Sygnathus scovelli (1768).  Dietary overlap is observed between the black sea bass, Centropristis striata, the southern porgy, Stenotomus aculeatus, and pinfish, though no indication of direct competition is seen (1737).  A strong similarity exists in feeding between pinfish and the mojarras, Eucinostomus gula and E. argenteus (1096).  The association between the pinfish and this genus has more to do with morphological similarity and not diet (1759).

Different food size selection in adults and habitat utilization differences in juveniles explain why pinfish and sheepshead, Archosargus probatocephalus, are not considered competitors, even though their food habits are similar (163 314).  By changing to benthic feeding habits, juvenile pinfish avoid competition with anchovies (1167).  Juveniles also avoid competition with other juvenile species because they enter estuaries months prior to the others (1167).

Predation:  The pinfish is an important prey fish for the larger, commercial and recreational species (1581).  Predators include:  fish -- ladyfish, Elops saurus; sandbar shark, Carcharhinus plumbeus; southern hake, Urophycis floridana; gulf toadfish, Opsanus beta; red drum, Scianenops ocellatus; spotted seatrout, Cynoscion nebulosus; sailfish, Istiophorus platypterus; weakfish, Cynoscion regalis; southern flounder, Paralichthys lethostigma;  aliigator gar, Lepisosteus spatula; longnose gar, Lepisosteus osseus; bighead searobin, Prionotus tribulus; marine mammals -- spotted dolphin, Stenella plagiodon; bottlenose dolphin, Tursiops truncatus; birds --  eastern brown pelican, Pelcanus occidentalis carolinensis; magnificent frigate bird, Fregata magnificens rothschildi; double-crested cormorant, Phalacrocorax a. auritus (312 163 581 1284 98 456 1347 1614 1615 1616 1617 1618 1619, all cited in 1581; 496 1554 1770).

Parasites/Diseases:  Parasites found from pinfish, listed in Caldwell (91), include:  protozoeans -- myxosporideans, found externally;  trematodes -- Pseudohaliotrema carbunculus, found on the gills; Leprocreadium ovalis, found in the intestine;  Lepidauchen hysterospine, found in the intestine;  Disomum monicellii, found in the intestine; D. appendiuculatum; D. vitellosum, found in the intestine; D. pyriforme; D. corpulentum; Diastomum sp.; Cymbephallus vitellosus; cestodes -- Scolex polymorphus, found in the intestine; Rhynchobothrium sp., found as visceral cysts; Otobothrium crenacolle, found as cysts; Tetrarhynchus bisulcatus, found as cysts; nematodes -- Ascaris sp., found in the body cavity;  acanthocephalans -- Echinirhynchus pristis, found in the intestine; E. sagittifer, found on viscera; copepods -- Caligus praetextus, found externally; Hatschekia linearis, found on the gills; Lernathropus amplitergum, found on the gills; Leraeenicus polyceraus, found externally; Argulus funduli; A. varians; malacostracans -- Agnatha medialis, found on the gills.  The isopod Lironeca ovalis and the haematozoan Haemogreyarina bigemina are also observed to effect the pinfish (1779 1780; as cited in 496)

Dermatological lesions resembling ulcerative mycosis were observed on pinfish of Tar-Pamlico estuary, North Carolina (1738).  Bacterial dermatitis and myositis, lymphocystis, Henneguya myositis, Argulus dermatitis, and various idiopathic dermatopathies were some other less prevalent dermatological diseases found in Tar-Pamlico (1738).
	In Alabama and Florida, Streptococcus sp. is considered the major disease effecting pinfish (1778, as cited in 496).

Perturbations: No information available.
Climate: No information available.
Other: No information available.

nodes.title: HUMAN IMPACTS
nodes.body:
Oil Spills: 10% mortality and depressed respiratory rates were observed in pinfish, due to petrochemical wastes at a Corpus Christi turning basin (1633).

Kloth and Wohlschlag (1786) studied the effect of salinity and 0.5% petrochemical effluent on the pinfish.  They found that the pollutant depressed metabolism in small fish at all salinities and large fish at 20 and 32 ppt.  However, this sublethal pollution elevated metabolism in large fish at a salinity of 45 ppt.

Contaminants:  The pinfish is a frequent and important species in pesticide, bioconcentration, acute toxicity, heavy metal, and other aquatic pollutant testing (1581).  When tested with sheepshead, croaker, and sea catfish, the pinfish was found to be the “least susceptible” to contaminant cupric chloride concentrations in an artificial seawater experiment (1742).  When exposed to the pesticide EPN, the pinfish showed a bioconcentration level 707 times that of the exposure water (1743).  When studying bleached kraft pulpmill effluent, Lewis and Livingston (1746) found that concentrations of 0.1% caused no avoidance in the pinfish, low avoidance at 0.1%, and marked avoidance at 1.0% and 10.0%.  The estimated avoidance threshold level was 0.06% (1746).

High concentrations of nickel and chromium were found in shrimp and pinfish located in the lower Laguna Madre, TX (1748).  Custer and Mitchell (1748) found this difficult to explain as these trace elements could not be linked to any anthropogenic sources.

When estuarine species were tested against the insecticide toxaphene, sheepshead minnows and pinfish were the most sensitive animals (1752).  Toxaphene was considered toxic to embryos, fry, juveniles, and adults, but fertilization was unaffected by tested amounts (1752).

Pinfish have shown to form abnormalities in Biscayne Bay, FL as contaminants in the environments are believed to have caused pugheadedness, jaw deformities, and other abnormalities (1758).  Deformities like these can result from an imbalance in calcium metaboloism, as heavy metals and chlorinated hydrocarbons, including PCBs, interfere with this process (1758).

Entrainment/Impingement: Young-of-year pinfish showed greater steady swimming and impingement avoidance at higher temperatures when tested on swimming performances against certain variables (1739).  Greater water velocities negatively affected pinfish ability to maintain steady swimming and impingement avoidance (1739).  At equal water velocities, larger fish had a faster maximum swimming speed and avoided impingement longer, but smaller individuals swam steadily for longer periods and showed stronger rheotaxis (1739).



Eutrophication:  No information available.

Pollutant Toxicity:  The pinfish is a frequent and important species in pesticide, bioconcentration, acute toxicity, heavy metal, and other aquatic pollutant testing (1581).  Pinfish are tolerant of somewhat high concentrations of bleached kraft mill effluent (1594).  Pollution in the water might be responsible for a decrease in respiration rate (1633; as cited in 1581).

Other:  Pinfish have been used extensively in bioassays (212 542 627) and physiological experiments (82 95 380 386).

sections.content:
Scientific Name:  Lagodon rhomboides

Synonyms: Taken from Darcy (1581):
	 	Sparus rhomboides, Linnaeus, 1766
		Sargus rhomboides, Valenciennes, in Cuvier and Valenciennes, 1830
		Diplodus rhomboides, Jordan and Gilbert, 1882
		Lagodon rhomboidalis, Goode and Bean, 1886
		Salema atkinsoni, Fowler, 1940
		Lagodon mercaroris, Delsman, 1941
Common Name: Pinfish
Other Common Names: Bream (particularly Florida Keys), salt-water bream (South Carolina), Fair-maid (Virginia), Spanish porgy (Bermuda), pin perch, sand perch, piggy-perch (parts of Western Gulf of Mexico), sailor`s choice, butterfish, chopa spina, chopa espina (Cuba), sargo (parts of the Florida Keys), sargo selema (Spanish), sar selema (French), poisson beurre (Cajun) (496 1581).
